anchors.fact: Before the 1950s, the drink "appears to have been" called simply *pinga com limão*, cane spirit with lime. It's on record only from the mid-nineteenth century: "of no great antiquity" (Oxford CAIPIRINHA, pdf 383). F2, F3
anchors.meaning: An everyday thing named after its ingredients. Keep Wondrich's "appears". Never "centuries-old", "ancient" or "traditional for generations". **Sugar isn't in the mid-1800s record:** the name is cane spirit *with lime*. The first sugar on the page is Wells's refresco of "cachaça, lemon, sugar, and water", thirty years after 1856 (1880s). So the mid-1800s date goes with the lime only (audit v2, A6).

anchors.fact: In São Paulo, in the first half of the 20th century, the Batida Paulista showed American influence ("not only in its incorporation of ice"). Some versions used simple syrup, others added egg white and a "splash" of gin, which the poet Mário de Andrade called "sophisticated" in 1944, and these "would require mixing in a cocktail shaker" (pdf 383). F4
anchors.meaning: The fashionable improvement, on the page. Syrup was in *some* versions, egg white and gin in *others*: never syrup as every version's touch (A7). **The shaker is tied to the egg white and gin only** (Tomás's anchor, r3): the page gives no method for the syrup versions or for the third way. Andrade's word reaches us in Wondrich's English, in quotation marks, and his tone is unknown: never a sneer, never praise. The improvers aren't sneered at either (Wren's test 4).
anchors.speaksTo: the fashionable try to improve it

anchors.fact: "Some drinkers, however, rejected such innovations" (pdf 383). F5
anchors.meaning: Someone said no to the additions. **Unknown:** who they were, why, and whether they're the people who made the caipirinha (Wren's note a). Any link is signposted.

anchors.fact: "A third way, one that incorporated the ice from the new drink into a nostalgic, rustic preparation built simply in the glass" (pdf 384). F6. **Contested:** Oxford's CACHAÇA entry calls the Batida Paulista "better known by its alternate name, the Caipirinha" (pdf 380), and Wondrich himself says "Batida Paulista" "appears to have been" one of its original names (pdf 383). C1
anchors.meaning: The heart of the mirror: it took the one new thing that was better (the cold) and left the show. Told as Wondrich's account ("as one historian tells it"), or after "I like to think". "Built simply in the glass" is a five-word run of his: in guest text, our words ("made right in the glass", A8). The page names the ice as what the third way took. "Just one thing" is our reading, and it lives in y3's "I like to think". "Nostalgic, rustic" is his reading: attribute it or put it in our own words. Never claim as fact that it was a separate drink from the city one.
anchors.speaksTo: takes the one better thing, leaves the show

anchors.fact: *Caipirinha* comes from *caipira*, "a southern Brazilian epithet for a person from the rural hinterlands". The name was in occasional use by the 1950s and widespread by the end of the 1960s, by which time the drink "was known throughout Brazil" (pdf 384). F7
anchors.meaning: Said once, plainly: "a word for someone from the countryside" (Wren's ruling). Never "Little Hillbilly", "affectionate" or "proud". Nobody on record chose the name or reclaimed the word, so the guest makes that link alone.

anchors.fact: Abroad, "a strong vogue in Europe ... where it remains popular" (pdf 384). Non-Brazilians consider it Brazil's national drink (pdf 383). F1, F8
anchors.meaning: No decade (1970s or 1980s is contested, C1). Never "the one the world orders" or "everywhere" (C2: the vodka version travelled too, as Kenya's Dawa, pdf 631). "National drink" is said from the outside only.

anchors.fact: "Fashionable city dwellers found cachaça too rustic and backward-looking" and preferred vodka: the Caipiroska, which "first appears in the early 1980s" (pdf 384). F9
anchors.meaning: The fashionable kept the name and dropped the cane. Said gently, with no sneer at the city or at vodka drinkers. "Early 1980s" is the first appearance, not the year everyone switched.

anchors.fact: Decree 4.851 (2 Oct 2003): a caipirinha is "a bebida típica brasileira", made "exclusivamente com Cachaça, acrescida de limão e açúcar". Decree 6.871 (2009, art. 68 §5): may be called caipirinha when "elaborada com cachaça, limão e açúcar". Decree 12.709 (31 Oct 2025, art. 74, in force): "industrializada", "elaborada com cachaça, limão e açúcar". L1–L3
anchors.meaning: Brazil set down in law that the name goes with the cane, the lime and the sugar. That vindicates it **as plain**. **Scope:** the decrees regulate drinks made and sold as products ("industrializada"), not what a bar or a kitchen pours. "Only"/"exclusively" is 2003's wording alone: the 2009 text allows water and additives. Never "banned" or "illegal". Safe line: *Brazil's law defines a caipirinha as cachaça, lime and sugar, and has since 2003.*
anchors.speaksTo: vindicated as plain; the emperor moment

anchors.fact: Cachaça: by the end of the 19th century "both loved for its deep traditions and scorned for its perceived rusticity and backwardness" (Oxford CACHAÇA, pdf 379). By Brazilian law it's 38–48% ABV (pdf 379; *Codex* p. 112). F10, F12
anchors.meaning: Loved and looked down on at the same time: the guest's position, in a bottle. Our words only.

anchors.fact: Granulated sugar muddled with lime "abrades the zest of the lime and introduces the lime's essential oils to the drink" (*Joy* pdf 173; pdf 151: "far fresher-tasting", said of lemons, "also occurs in a Caipirinha"). The muddled lime stays in: "a pleasant limy flavor that builds toward the end", though the pieces "can get bitter" (*Codex* p. 137).
anchors.meaning: The taste reason for the sugar and the lime left in (Tomás's guard: never a history reason). "Fresher" is Regan's word for the effect. Our build in the glass with no shaker is **our** reading of "built simply in the glass", not a documented recipe. The *Codex* shakes its own version.

anchors.fact: *Codex* p. 115: the peel holds "the bitter pith"; "if a seedy piece of citrus is muddled, the drink can become quite bitter". *Joy* pdf 263: muddle limes and sugar in an old-fashioned glass, add crushed ice and cachaça, stir.
anchors.meaning: The seed step and the peel's bitterness are sourced. Muddling in the glass has a book behind it (*Joy*), so the build isn't only our invention; the third way's own method still isn't on any page.

anchors.fact: Ours: unaged cachaça (our choice; the law says only "cachaça", A9), a medium lime (6 of 8 pieces), granulated sugar, cracked ice, built and stirred in the glass.
anchors.meaning: It matches the law's three things plus the ice the third way kept. Never "the original recipe" or "the way Brazilians make it": no period recipe with measures is on the page. Never say our glass "meets the law" (the decrees cover products).

cocktail.closingLine: Leave the lime in. Then let the whole table see you enjoying it.
cocktail.glassware: rocks glass (double old-fashioned, about 300 ml), filled with cracked ice
method: Cut the lime in half across the middle. Lay each half cut side down and cut it into quarters. Pick out any seeds you can see, because they make it bitter.
Put 6 of the pieces in a sturdy rocks glass and add the sugar. Keep the last 2 pieces for the next one.
Press each piece firmly with a muddler, or the end of a rolling pin, giving it a slight twist, until every piece is crushed and the sugar has mostly gone. Then stop.
Fill the glass with cracked ice. To crack it, wrap ice cubes in a clean tea towel and give them a few knocks with the rolling pin.
Pour in the cachaça and stir from the bottom for about ten seconds, so the sugar comes up into the drink.
Leave the lime pieces in. They keep flavouring the drink, and the peel can add a little bitterness, which is part of the pleasure.
cocktail.name: Good as It Is

recipe.note: white (prata or branca), any bottle of 38–45%: the cane spirit itself
cut across the middle, then each half into quarters; 6 of the 8 pieces go in
grains, not syrup: they grind the oil out of the lime skin, so you taste the skin as well as the juice

cocktail.tagline: Impressing you is hard. Delighting you is easy.

reading.epigraph: In Brazil, the law spells out what goes in a caipirinha. It's a short list.
whoYouAre: At the wedding with seven courses and a little card for each, what you remember is the bread. Warm, with too much butter. You said so with your mouth still full, and you meant it. You know what the foam on the fish was meant to be. You've heard the words, and you can use them if you have to. You just liked the bread more.

What stings isn't being called plain. It's the half-smile that says you liked it because you don't know any better. So in some rooms you turn yourself down a notch, and more than once you've ordered the clever thing just to keep your seat at the table. That costs you more than it shows. What you're really afraid of is being let in as the sweet one, and never as one of them. But watch what happens on the nights you don't turn it down. Someone leans over and admits the bread was the best bit for them too. Then someone else does. It's worth more than it looks: with you there, people can stop performing and just enjoy it.
yours: Brazilians were already drinking cachaça, their spirit made from sugar cane, with lime by the middle of the 1800s. In the first half of the last century, the city of São Paulo gave it American touches: ice, and in some versions sugar syrup, or egg white and a splash of gin, which the poet Mário de Andrade described in 1944 as "sophisticated". Some drinkers turned the new touches down.

As one historian tells it, a third way came out of that: the old country drink, made right in the glass, taking the ice from the city version. It took the name caipirinha, from a word for someone from the countryside, and by the end of the 1960s it was known all over Brazil. Europe took to it later, and still loves it. Back home, the fashionable city crowd found cachaça too rustic and made the drink with vodka instead. Brazil's law, though, defines a caipirinha as cachaça, lime and sugar, and has since 2003.

I like to think the people who kept it plain knew exactly what the egg white and gin would do, and took the ice because cold is simply better, and left the rest because they liked it how it was. You choose the same way. You're not against new things. You take what's actually good and leave the show.

The cocktail I've made for you is the caipirinha, Brazil's famous classic, made with just three things, the same three its law names: cachaça, lime and sugar, and then the ice. The cachaça is an unaged one. I didn't add anything, as a nod to the people who kept it plain. I built it in the glass with no shaker, which is how I picture that third way. The sugar is crushed into most of a lime until it has nearly gone, and its grains scrub the oil from the skin, so you taste the skin as well as the juice. The sugar stays on the dry side, so the cane and the lime come through. The pieces stay in, peel and all, and if it's left to sit, the peel adds a little bitterness. It's cold, bright and sharp, with the cane spirit's warmth underneath.

A small dare, then. Next time a table goes quiet and careful over something clever, don't wait to hear what everyone else thought. Say what you loved, even if it was the bread. It'll be a better evening for it, and you'll learn how many of them were hoping someone would.
